lessons.title: Developing a Project Charter
lessons.body:
A project charter is a one- to two-page document that formally authorizes your project and gives you, the project manager, the authority to use organizational resources. In an African context, where many projects run on tight budgets and informal agreements, a charter prevents misunderstandings. For example, if you are launching a poultry farm in Ghana with a budget of 50,000 Ghanaian cedis, the charter states the goal, budget, timeline, and key stakeholders. Without it, you risk scope creep or funding disputes.

To develop a charter, start by talking to the project sponsorâthe person or group providing the money. Ask: What problem are we solving? What does success look like? What is the deadline? Then draft the charter using a simple template. Include: project title, purpose, measurable objectives (e.g., 'produce 1,000 eggs per week by month 6'), high-level scope, key deliverables, budget, timeline, major risks, and approval signatures. Use tools like Google Docs or Microsoft Word; if offline, a notebook works. In rural areas, you might use a chalkboard to outline the charter with your team.

Keep the charter practical. For a solar panel installation project in Kenya, the charter might list: install 20 panels in 3 schools by December, budget 800,000 Kenyan shillings, sponsor: County Education Office. Avoid jargon. Write in plain language that a farmer or shop owner can understand. Circulate the draft to the sponsor and key stakeholders for feedback. Once approved, the charter becomes your reference pointâany change request must be checked against it.

Finally, store the charter where everyone can access it. In low-connectivity areas, print copies and post them at the project site. Review it at every team meeting to keep everyone aligned. A good charter takes 2-3 hours to draft and saves weeks of confusion later.

lessons.title: Identifying Business Needs and Benefits
lessons.body:
Before you start any project, you must clearly identify the business needâthe problem or opportunity that justifies spending time and money. In Africa, common needs include increasing income, reducing costs, meeting regulatory requirements, or improving community services. For instance, a cassava processing cooperative in Nigeria might need a new grinding machine because manual grinding takes 5 hours per 100 kg, limiting production to 200 kg per day. The need is faster processing; the benefit is higher output and profit.

To identify needs, talk to customers, staff, and community members. Use simple tools like a needs assessment survey or a focus group. Ask: What is not working? What is costing us money? What opportunities are we missing? For a mobile money agent in Uganda, a need might be reducing customer wait time from 15 minutes to 5 minutes. Quantify the need: how many customers are lost per day due to waiting? Multiply by average transaction fee to estimate lost revenue.

Benefits must be measurable and tied to the need. Use a benefits map: need â project output â outcome â benefit. For example, need: high post-harvest losses (30% of tomatoes). Output: solar-powered cold storage. Outcome: tomatoes last 10 days instead of 3. Benefit: increase income by 40% for 50 farmers. Write these in your charter. Also consider dis-benefits, like the cost of maintenance or training.

Involve the sponsor early to validate the need and benefits. A sponsor from a microfinance bank will want to see return on investment. For a 200,000 Kenyan shilling cold storage unit, show that it will save 500,000 shillings in losses per year. Document everything in a one-page business case. This prevents pet projects that waste resources. Remember: if you cannot state the need in one sentence and the benefit in numbers, the project is not ready to start.

lessons.title: Conducting Stakeholder Analysis
lessons.body:
Stakeholders are anyone who affects or is affected by your project. In African projects, stakeholders often include funders, local government, community leaders, suppliers, and end-users. Missing a key stakeholder can stall your projectâfor example, not consulting a village chief before building a borehole in Tanzania can lead to resistance. Stakeholder analysis helps you identify who matters, what they care about, and how to engage them.

Start by listing all potential stakeholders. Use a simple brainstorming session with your team. Then classify them using a power/interest grid: high power, high interest (manage closely); high power, low interest (keep satisfied); low power, high interest (keep informed); low power, low interest (monitor). For a school feeding project in Malawi, the Ministry of Education has high power and high interestâmeet monthly. Parents have high interest but low powerâsend weekly SMS updates. Suppliers have low interest but high power over deliveryâsign clear contracts.

Next, understand each stakeholder's needs and concerns. Interview them or hold a meeting. For a solar mini-grid project in Ethiopia, the community may worry about affordability; the utility company may worry about grid stability. Document these in a stakeholder register: name, role, contact, expectations, influence level, and engagement strategy. Use Excel or a notebook. In low-literacy contexts, use pictures or symbols.

Finally, plan engagement. For high-power stakeholders, schedule face-to-face meetings. For high-interest groups, use community radio or WhatsApp groups. Assign a team member to each key stakeholder. Review the register monthly. A good analysis takes 1-2 days but prevents costly delays. For example, in a road construction project in Rwanda, engaging the local transport cooperative early avoided a week-long protest that would have cost 5 million Rwandan francs.

lessons.title: Defining High-Level Scope and Deliverables
lessons.body:
Scope defines what your project will and will not do. Deliverables are the tangible outputs you promise to produce. In African projects, vague scope leads to endless extra workâlike a 'community garden' that becomes a farm, a training center, and a market stall. To avoid this, write a scope statement: project objective, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, and constraints.

Start with the objective. For a fish farming project in Uganda, the objective might be 'increase tilapia production by 2 tonnes per year for 10 farmers by December 2025.' Then list deliverables: 10 fish ponds (each 10m x 10m), a training manual, 5,000 fingerlings, and a harvesting plan. Each deliverable must be specific and measurable. Use a work breakdown structure (WBS) to break deliverables into smaller tasks. For example, 'fish ponds' becomes: site survey, excavation, lining, water inlet, and fencing. A WBS can be drawn on paper or using free tools like Trello or Google Sheets.

Define acceptance criteria: how will you know a deliverable is complete? For a pond, it must hold water without leaking for 48 hours, be at least 1.5m deep, and have a secure inlet. Exclusions are equally important: 'This project does not include fish processing or marketing.' Constraints include budget (e.g., 15 million Ugandan shillings), timeline (6 months), and resources (only 2 excavators available).

Share the scope with stakeholders and get sign-off. In many African contexts, verbal agreement is common, but insist on a written scope to prevent disputes. If a stakeholder asks for an extra deliverable, refer to the exclusions. For example, if a local leader asks for a borehole as part of the fish project, politely explain it is out of scope. Document any approved changes. A clear scope reduces rework by up to 30% and keeps your project on track.

lessons.title: Assembling the Project Team
lessons.body:
Your project team is the group of people who will do the work. In Africa, teams are often small and multi-skilled. For a 6-month project, you might need a project manager, a technical expert, a community liaison, and a part-time accountant. Assemble the team based on skills, not just availability. For a solar installation in Senegal, you need a certified electrician, a roofer, and a local translator. Avoid hiring friends who lack skillsâit leads to failure.

Start by defining roles and responsibilities. Use a simple RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for each major task. For a market research project in Kenya, the data collector is Responsible for surveys, the project manager is Accountable, the sponsor is Consulted, and the community is Informed. Write this in a table. Then recruit. Use local networks: community meetings, WhatsApp groups, technical colleges. For a 3-month project, you might pay a stipend of 20,000 Kenyan shillings per month for a data collector.

Consider cultural dynamics. In many African settings, age and seniority matter. A young project manager may need to respectfully involve elders. Build trust through tea meetings or site visits. Also plan for training: if you hire a local farmer to operate a rice thresher, budget 2 days for training. For remote teams, use free tools like WhatsApp for daily check-ins and Google Drive for file sharing. If internet is poor, use SMS updates.

Finally, document team agreements: working hours, payment schedule, and conflict resolution. For a 10-person team in Ghana, a simple written contract (even handwritten) prevents disputes. Assign a deputy for each key role to cover absences. A well-assembled team can double productivity. For example, a cassava processing team in Nigeria with clear roles reduced processing time from 8 hours to 3 hours per tonne.

lessons.title: Obtaining Formal Project Approval
lessons.body:
Formal approval is the official green light to start your project. Without it, you risk working without authority or funding. In African contexts, approval may come from a donor, a government office, or a community board. For a water sanitation project in Ethiopia, approval might require signatures from the woreda (district) water bureau and the kebele (neighborhood) chairman. The process can take days or weeks, so plan for it.

To obtain approval, prepare a approval package: the project charter, business case, stakeholder register, scope statement, and team list. Present it in a meeting or submit it in writing. For a 500,000 Ethiopian birr project, the donor may require a formal letter of request. Use a simple cover letter stating: project title, duration, budget, expected benefits, and request for approval. Attach supporting documents. If possible, get verbal support first from key decision-makers to smooth the process.

Understand the approval criteria. Donors often look for sustainability, community contribution, and clear metrics. For example, a grant for a poultry project in Tanzania might require a 10% community contribution and a plan for selling eggs. Address these in your proposal. If approval is delayed, follow up politely every 3 days. In some cases, you may need to adjust the budget or timeline. Be flexible but protect the core scope.

Once approved, get signatures on the charter. Scan or photograph the signed document and share it with your team. Announce the approval to stakeholders via a meeting or SMS. Then start work immediatelyâmomentum matters. For a 6-month project, a 2-week delay in approval can push harvest into a dry season, reducing yields. Keep a copy of the approval in your project file. Formal approval not only authorizes work but also builds trust with your community and funders.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Project Initiation and Chartering in African Agribusiness

In African agribusiness, projects rarely fail because of poor execution alone. More often, they fail at the starting line: a cassava processing plant is built without secured feedstock supply, an irrigation scheme is designed without confirming land tenure, or a cooperative warehouse is commissioned without a signed offtake agreement. Project initiation is the discipline that prevents these failures. It is the phase where a business need is translated into a funded, authorised, and resourced project with a clear mandate. This practical reference lesson consolidates the six lessons of this module into a working toolkit you can apply to any agricultural project, from a 5-hectare greenhouse in Kenya to a cross-border grain trading platform in West Africa.

1. The Initiation Logic: From Business Need to Charter

Project initiation follows a logical sequence. First, you identify and validate a business need or opportunity â for example, a poultry cooperative in Ghana losing 18% of birds to Newcastle disease because it lacks cold-chain storage. Second, you conduct a stakeholder analysis to understand who is affected, who has influence, and who must approve. Third, you define high-level scope and deliverables â what the project will and will not do. Fourth, you assemble the core project team. Fifth, you develop the project charter, which formally authorises the project and gives the project manager authority to apply organisational resources. Finally, you obtain formal approval from the sponsor or governing body.

The charter is not a detailed plan. It is a high-level authorising document. In agribusiness, it should explicitly address seasonality, weather risk, input supply, land access, and market linkage â the five factors that most often derail agricultural projects in Africa.

2. Developing the Project Charter

A project charter in agribusiness must answer seven questions: Why are we doing this? What will success look like? Who is the sponsor? Who is the project manager and what authority do they have? What is in scope and out of scope? What are the major milestones aligned to the agricultural calendar? What is the high-level budget and funding source? The charter should be one to three pages â not a business plan. It is signed by the sponsor, not the project manager.

For example, a dairy cooperative in Uganda chartering a milk chilling hub would specify: purpose (reduce spoilage from 22% to below 8%), sponsor (cooperative board), project manager (operations manager with authority to procure up to UGX 50 million), scope (chiller installation, solar backup, collection route design), out of scope (retail outlet construction), milestones tied to dry and wet seasons, and budget of UGX 420 million with 60% grant and 40% cooperative equity.

3. Identifying Business Needs and Benefits

Business needs in African agribusiness usually fall into five categories: productivity gaps, post-harvest losses, market access constraints, financing gaps, and compliance requirements. Benefits must be measurable and tied to a baseline. A common mistake is stating benefits in vague terms such as "improve livelihoods." Instead, state: "Increase smallholder maize yields from 1.8 t/ha to 2.6 t/ha within two seasons for 1,200 farmers in Nakuru County."

Table 1: Common Agribusiness Needs and Measurable Benefit Statements
Business Need Category Example (Africa) Measurable Benefit Statement
Productivity gap Low sorghum yields in northern Nigeria Increase yields from 1.1 t/ha to 1.9 t/ha for 3,000 farmers by 2027
Post-harvest loss Tomato spoilage in Tanzania Reduce post-harvest loss from 35% to 12% through cold storage
Market access Smallholder coffee in Ethiopia Secure offtake contracts for 500 MT at premium of 18% above farmgate
Financing gap Input credit for rice farmers in Senegal Provide seasonal credit to 800 farmers with 95% repayment rate
Compliance GlobalG.A.P. certification for Kenyan exporters Achieve certification for 12 exporter groups within 18 months

Source: Compiled from FAO, Project Cycle Management Technical Guide, 2021; and AGRA, Africa Agriculture Status Report 2022.

4. Conducting Stakeholder Analysis

Stakeholder analysis in agribusiness must go beyond a simple list. Use a powerâinterest grid and record each stakeholder's stake, influence, attitude, and engagement strategy. In African agricultural projects, critical stakeholders often include smallholder farmers, cooperatives, input suppliers, off-takers, transporters, local government, traditional authorities, regulators, financiers, and community groups. Traditional authorities and community elders are frequently overlooked but can block or enable land access and labour mobilisation.

Table 2: Stakeholder Analysis Register Template (Agribusiness Example)
Stakeholder Stake / Interest Power (H/M/L) Attitude Engagement Strategy
Smallholder farmers Inputs, fair price, timely payment M Supportive if paid on time Farmer field days, transparent pricing
Cooperative board Governance, member benefit H Supportive Monthly reporting, board representation
Off-taker / buyer Quality, volume, delivery schedule H Neutral to supportive Contract negotiation, quality audits
Local government Compliance, local employment M Neutral Permits, community meetings
Traditional authority Land, community consent H Neutral Early consultation, protocol respect
Financier / bank Repayment, risk management H Conditional Milestone-based disbursement, reporting

Source: Adapted from PMI, PMBOK Guide, 7th ed., 2021; and IFAD, Stakeholder Engagement in Rural Development Projects, 2020.

5. Defining High-Level Scope and Deliverables

Scope defines the boundary of the project. In agribusiness, scope must be explicit about geographic coverage, number of beneficiaries, crop or livestock value chain, and time horizon. Deliverables should be tangible and verifiable: a signed offtake contract, an installed cold room, a trained cohort of 200 farmers, a functioning MIS, a certification certificate. Avoid scope statements that cannot be verified.

A useful technique is the "in-scope / out-of-scope" table. For a sesame export project in Ethiopia, in-scope might include aggregation, cleaning, grading, and export documentation; out-of-scope might include primary production and international freight. This clarity prevents scope creep, which is the most common cause of budget overrun in agricultural projects.

6. Assembling the Project Team

The core team for an agribusiness project typically includes a project manager, an agronomist or value-chain specialist, a finance officer, a monitoring and evaluation (M&E) officer, a logistics or procurement officer, and a community engagement officer. In smaller projects, roles are combined. The charter should name the project manager and state their authority level, especially for procurement and hiring.

Team assembly must consider seasonality. If the project requires farmer mobilisation before the planting season, the community engagement officer must be recruited and deployed at least two months before rains. Delayed recruitment is a silent killer of agricultural project timelines.

7. Obtaining Formal Project Approval

Approval is a governance event, not a formality. The sponsor, board, or funding committee signs the charter, thereby authorising the project and releasing the initial budget. In donor-funded projects, approval may also require a no-objection from the funding agency. Without formal approval, the project manager has no authority to commit resources, and any spending is unauthorised.

â  SAFETY AND COMPLIANCE WARNING

Do not commence project activities, procure inputs, or mobilise farmers before the charter is formally signed. In African agribusiness, starting without approval exposes the project to: (a) personal liability for the project manager, (b) loss of donor funding due to ineligible expenditure, (c) breach of cooperative or company governance rules, and (d) reputational damage with communities who may have been promised benefits. If an urgent seasonal window requires early action, obtain written conditional approval from the sponsor and document it in the charter annex. Never rely on verbal approval.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Business need validated: Baseline data collected and benefit statement is measurable.
  • Stakeholder register complete: Power, interest, attitude, and engagement strategy recorded for all key actors, including traditional authorities.
  • Scope defined: In-scope and out-of-scope lists agreed and documented.
  • Deliverables listed: Each deliverable is tangible, verifiable, and time-bound.
  • Project manager named: Authority level for procurement and hiring stated in the charter.
  • Core team identified: Roles, names, and deployment dates aligned to the agricultural calendar.
  • Budget and funding source confirmed: High-level budget with funding split and disbursement milestones.
  • Charter signed by sponsor: Formal written approval obtained before any activity begins.

Further Reading

  • PMI â A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide)
  • FAO â Project Cycle Management Technical Guide
  • IFAD â Stakeholder Engagement in Rural Development Projects
  • AGRA â Africa Agriculture Status Report
  • African Development Bank â Project Documents and Guidelines

This lesson is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course on Project Management. It is designed for practitioners working in African agribusiness and rural development contexts.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a project charter?
options: A) To list all project tasks in detail
B) To formally authorize the project and give the project manager authority
D) To replace a business case
quiz.explanation: The charter formally authorizes the project and grants the project manager authority to use resources.

quiz.q: Which of the following should be included in a project charter?
quiz.explanation: Measurable objectives are a key component of a charter, while detailed schedules come later.

quiz.q: In an African context, why is a written charter especially important?
options: A) It replaces the need for a sponsor
B) It prevents misunderstandings in informal agreements
D) It is required by law in all countries
quiz.explanation: A written charter reduces ambiguity when many agreements are verbal or informal.

quiz.q: How long does it typically take to draft a good project charter?
quiz.explanation: A practical charter can be drafted in 2-3 hours with input from the sponsor.

quiz.q: What is the first step in identifying a business need?
options: B) Talk to customers and staff
quiz.explanation: Talking to stakeholders helps uncover the real problem or opportunity.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a measurable benefit?
options: B) Increase income by 40% for 50 farmers
quiz.explanation: Measurable benefits are quantifiable, like a 40% income increase for a specific group.

quiz.q: What tool can help map needs to benefits?
quiz.explanation: A benefits map links needs to outputs, outcomes, and benefits.

quiz.q: Why is it important to involve the sponsor early in identifying needs?
options: B) To validate the need and benefits
quiz.explanation: Sponsors validate that the need is real and the benefits justify the investment.

quiz.q: What is a dis-benefit?
options: A) A negative outcome of a project
quiz.explanation: Dis-benefits are negative consequences, like maintenance costs or training time.

quiz.q: If you cannot state the need in one sentence and the benefit in numbers, what should you do?
options: B) Delay the project until clarified
C) Ask the sponsor to write it
quiz.explanation: A project without a clear need and measurable benefit is not ready to start.

quiz.q: What is a stakeholder?
options: B) Anyone who affects or is affected by the project
quiz.explanation: Stakeholders include anyone with an interest or influence on the project.

quiz.q: Which tool helps classify stakeholders by power and interest?
quiz.explanation: The power/interest grid categorizes stakeholders based on their influence and concern.

quiz.q: For a stakeholder with high power and high interest, what is the best strategy?
quiz.explanation: High power and high interest stakeholders require close management.

quiz.q: What should a stakeholder register include?
options: B) Name, role, expectations, influence, engagement strategy
quiz.explanation: A stakeholder register documents key information to plan engagement.

quiz.q: Why is it important to engage local leaders in African projects?
options: B) They can stall the project if not consulted
C) They are always the sponsors
D) They do the technical work
quiz.explanation: Local leaders often have high power and can create resistance if ignored.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a scope statement?
options: A) To define what the project will and will not do
B) To list all team members
quiz.explanation: The scope statement clarifies boundaries and prevents scope creep.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a deliverable?
quiz.explanation: Deliverables are tangible outputs, like 10 fish ponds.

quiz.q: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
options: A) A hierarchical decomposition of deliverables into tasks
quiz.explanation: A WBS breaks down deliverables into smaller, manageable tasks.

quiz.q: What are acceptance criteria?
options: A) Conditions that must be met for a deliverable to be accepted
quiz.explanation: Acceptance criteria define how a deliverable will be judged complete.

quiz.q: Why are exclusions important in a scope statement?
options: A) They list what is not included, preventing misunderstandings
B) They list what is included
C) They list the team members
quiz.explanation: Exclusions clarify boundaries and prevent stakeholders from expecting out-of-scope work.

quiz.q: What is a constraint in project scope?
options: A) A limitation such as budget, timeline, or resources
quiz.explanation: Constraints are restrictions that affect how the project can be done.

quiz.q: What should you do if a stakeholder asks for an extra deliverable not in scope?
options: B) Refer to the exclusions and explain it is out of scope
D) Ask the team to do it unpaid
quiz.explanation: Referring to the scope statement helps manage requests and prevent scope creep.

quiz.q: What is the first step in assembling a project team?
quiz.explanation: Defining roles and responsibilities ensures clarity before recruitment.

quiz.q: What does RACI stand for?
quiz.explanation: RACI is a matrix that clarifies roles for each task.

quiz.q: Why is cultural sensitivity important when assembling a team in Africa?
options: A) It ensures everyone is paid equally
B) It builds trust and respects age/seniority dynamics
C) It reduces the need for training
quiz.explanation: Respecting cultural norms, such as age and seniority, helps build a cohesive team.

quiz.q: What is a practical way to communicate with a remote team with poor internet?
quiz.explanation: SMS is reliable in low-connectivity areas and can keep the team updated.

quiz.q: What should be documented in team agreements?
options: A) Working hours, payment schedule, conflict resolution
quiz.explanation: Clear agreements prevent disputes and set expectations.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of assigning a deputy for each key role?
options: B) It covers absences and builds redundancy
quiz.explanation: Deputies ensure continuity when the primary person is unavailable.

quiz.q: What is formal project approval?
options: B) Official authorization to start the project
quiz.explanation: Formal approval gives the green light and often involves signatures.

quiz.q: What should an approval package include?
options: B) Charter, business case, stakeholder register, scope statement, team list
quiz.explanation: A comprehensive package helps decision-makers evaluate the project.

quiz.q: Why is it important to get verbal support before formal approval?
options: B) It smooths the approval process
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Verbal support from key decision-makers can expedite formal approval.

quiz.q: What should you do if approval is delayed?
options: B) Follow up politely every 3 days
quiz.explanation: Polite follow-up keeps the process moving without damaging relationships.

quiz.q: What is a common approval criterion for donors?
options: C) The number of team members
D) The color of the charter
quiz.explanation: Donors often look for sustainability and local contribution to ensure long-term impact.

quiz.q: After approval, what should you do with the signed charter?
options: A) File it away and forget it
B) Share it with the team and stakeholders
quiz.explanation: Sharing the approved charter keeps everyone aligned and informed.

quiz.q: Why does a delay in approval matter for a 6-month agricultural project?
options: B) It can push harvest into a dry season, reducing yields
D) It gives more time for planning
quiz.explanation: Timing is critical in agriculture; delays can miss optimal planting or harvest windows.
